newsitem.title: JAPAN: Major parties, key figures in Japan election.
newsitem.headline: Major parties, key figures in Japan election.

text.p: Major parties and key figures in Sunday's elections for the Lower House of Japan's parliament:
LIBERAL DEMOCRATIC PARTY (LDP) - Seats in outgoing Lower House: 211.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's conservative LDP ruled for 38 years until being ousted by a reformist coalition in August 1993, then returned to power in a coalition government less than a year later. It is in a commanding position to continue its rule, whether alone or in a new coalition. Most voter surveys in the past week have predicted that Hashimoto's party will win a majority of the 500 seats.
The LDP platform says it would raise a controversial sales tax to five percent from three percent next year, but would at the same time streamline the bloated bureaucracy.

Key players include the forceful Seiroku Kajiyama, who has favoured a grand alliance with the main opposition Shinshinto, as well as Koichi Kato, who has been keen on keeping the current alliance with the so-called "liberal" force of the Social Democrats and Sakigake, and with the fledgling Democratic Party. Even if it won an outright majority in the Lower House, the LDP might still try to form a coalition because it does not hold a majority in the Upper House.
SHINSHINTO (NEW FRONTIER PARTY): Seats in outgoing house: 160.

Since its foundation in a merger of nine opposition parties in December 1994, Shinshinto has become the country's main opposition group. It is headed by former LDP strongman Ichiro Ozawa. Since winning most votes in Upper House elections last year, it has steadily lost steam and faces serious splits between conservatives and reformists.

Ozawa has tried to prop up the party's sagging fortunes and boost chances of overtaking the LDP with drastic campaign promises, including an 18 trillion yen ($161 billion) income tax cut, scrapping the sales tax rise, a 25 percent reduction in bureaucrats and radical decentralisation. But voter surveys suggest Shinshinto will struggle to keep its current strength.
DEMOCRATIC PARTY of JAPAN (DJP): Seats in outgoing house: 52.

This new liberal party was formed on September 28, mostly from members of the two small parties in the ruling coalition -- the Social Democrats and Sakigake. It is led by Yukio Hatoyama, the scion of a family that has produced three generations of well-known politicians, and Health Minister Naoto Kan, who saw his popularity surge after he made good on a promise to open up a 10-year-old scandal at his ministry involving blood products tainted with HIV, the virus that causes AIDS. If the LDP becomes the largest party after voting day but fails to win a majority of seats, the Democrats could hold the balance of power. The latest media polls say the Democrats are headed for about 50 to 60 seats.
SOCIAL DEMOCRATIC PARTY (SDP): Seats in outgoing house: 30.

In 1994, under Tomiichi Murayama, the party formed a coalition government with its longtime foe the LDP, ditching its opposition to the U.S.-Japan Security Treaty and Japan's postwar military. Since then, however, the party has split between diehard leftists and a moderate right wing, the latter finally joining Hatoyama's Democratic Party last month. Murayama then offered the party leadership to Takako Doi, Japan's best-known woman politician and outgoing Lower House Speaker. The SDP faces major losses or even extinction in the election.
JAPAN COMMUNIST PARTY (JCP): Seats in outgoing house: 15.

The Communists, Japan's oldest political party, may benefit from the split in the Social Democrats by garnering the pacifist vote and could double its strength, but has steadfastly refused to join in any coalition.
SAKIGAKE: Seats in outgoing house: nine.

The party that suffered most from the emergence of Hatoyama's Democrats, Sakigake is in danger of becoming one of a handful of minor parties. Unpopular former finance minister Masayoshi Takemura resigned as party head after he failed to win agreement to merge his party with Hatoyama's new group. It is now led by little-known former health minister Shoichi Ide. ($1=112 yen)
